value.overview: The Lovely Cotinga (Cotinga amabilis) is a striking, fruit-eating forest bird of Mexico and Central America. Adult males are vivid turquoise-blue, while females and immature birds are brownish and finely marked. It usually stays high in the forest canopy, where its quiet behavior and preference for isolated perches can make it difficult to find. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon and localized species associated mainly with humid forest and mature forest edges.
value.classification: The Lovely Cotinga belongs to the cotinga family, Cotingidae, within the order Passeriformes. It is one of several brightly colored canopy-dwelling cotingas found in the Neotropics.
value.identification: The adult male is a medium-sized, compact cotinga with brilliant blue to turquoise plumage, darker wings and tail, and a contrasting dark facial area. Females and immature birds are much less colorful, with grayish-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and darker spotting or scalloped feather edges. Both sexes have a short, broad bill and dark eyes, legs, and feet. The species is often detected as a blue bird perched openly near the canopy rather than by its voice.
value.rangeHabitat: The Lovely Cotinga ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica, with occasional records farther south. In Costa Rica it is uncommon and has been recorded mainly on the Caribbean slope, although sightings also occur on the Pacific side. It occupies humid lowland and foothill evergreen forest, forest interiors and edges, and more open areas retaining scattered mature trees. In Costa Rica it can occur from near sea level to roughly 1,700 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Generally considered a year-round resident, although some seasonal movements may occur. In Costa Rica it is present as an uncommon resident or regularly occurring species rather than a predictable long-distance migrant; local movements may follow fruiting trees and changing food availability.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Lovely Cotinga remains poorly known. Available observations suggest that nesting takes place high in trees, including in the canopy and in tall pines. Nest construction has not been well documented, and few details are available about courtship, clutch size, incubation, or parental care. One observed female provisioned a flightless nestling. In Costa Rica, breeding information is especially limited, so the timing and frequency of nesting there remain uncertain.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is thought to consist mainly of fruits, supplemented by invertebrates and possibly occasional small vertebrates such as lizards. It usually forages alone or in pairs in the upper canopy, perching on exposed branches before making short flights to take fruit or capture prey. Several individuals may gather at a productive fruiting tree. Its dependence on mature fruiting trees links its feeding success closely to the condition of forest habitat.
value.behavior: Lovely Cotingas are usually quiet and inconspicuous despite the male's bright color. They often sit motionless on exposed canopy branches and make short, direct sallies for food. Males may give faint, high-pitched metallic notes, while the wings can produce a dry rattling sound in flight. The species is most often seen singly or in pairs, though temporary groups may form where food is abundant.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing, although the size and speed of the decline are not well quantified.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is loss and fragmentation of mature tropical forest through agricultural expansion, cattle grazing, and other land conversion. Removal of large fruiting trees may reduce feeding opportunities and may also affect breeding habitat. Because the species is uncommon and its biology is poorly known, local declines can be difficult to detect.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining humid forests and maintain connected habitat between forest blocks, especially on Costa Rica's Caribbean slope. Retain large native fruiting trees in reserves, farms, and restoration areas, limit further forest clearing, and support protected-area management. Carefully documented sightings submitted to established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of the species' distribution, seasonal movements, and population changes.
